Homeopathy is a system of alternative medicine based on the belief that the body can heal itself, and that extremely diluted substances can stimulate that healing process.

The word is used to describe both the system of practice and the philosophy behind it. When someone says "I tried homeopathy for my cold," they mean they used this particular approach to treatment — not conventional medicine, but this specific alternative system.
The Two Beliefs It Rests On

Homeopathy is built on two central claims:

1. "Like cures like."
This is the idea that a substance which causes certain symptoms in a healthy person can cure those same symptoms in a sick person. For example, since caffeine causes sleeplessness, a homeopath might use a caffeine-based remedy to treat insomnia.

2. The more diluted, the stronger.
This is where homeopathy becomes especially distinctive — and controversial. Practitioners believe that diluting a substance in water, repeatedly, makes it more powerful as a medicine, not weaker. The original substance is diluted many times over, and each time, the solution is shaken vigorously (a process called "succussion"). Homeopaths believe this shaking transfers the "memory" or "essence" of the substance into the water, even after the original substance is essentially gone.

In practice, many homeopathic remedies are diluted so many times that mathematically, not even a single molecule of the original substance remains in the final product. A common dilution level is "30C," which means the substance was diluted by a factor of 10 to the power of 60 — an almost incomprehensibly small concentration.

You'll typically find them sold as small white sugar pellets, liquid drops, or tablets. They're widely available in pharmacies and health stores, often packaged like regular medicine. Labels might say things like "Arnica 30C" or "Belladonna 200C" — the letter and number refer to the dilution level. They're used for a wide range of complaints: coughs, anxiety, allergies, headaches, grief, insomnia, and many more.
How the Scientific and Medical World Views It

Here is where accuracy demands directness: mainstream science and medicine regard homeopathy as a pseudoscience. That means it presents itself with the language and appearance of medicine, but it lacks scientific foundation.

The core problems are:

  • No plausible mechanism. Modern chemistry and physics give us no reason to believe water can "remember" a substance, or that extreme dilution increases potency. The opposite is true in all of established science.
  • No reliable evidence of effectiveness. Dozens of large, well-designed clinical trials and systematic reviews — conducted across different countries and institutions — have consistently found that homeopathic treatments perform no better than a placebo (a sugar pill with no active ingredient). When people improve after using homeopathy, researchers attribute it to the placebo effect, the natural course of illness resolving on its own, or other lifestyle factors.
  • Major health authorities reject it. Organisations like the World Health Organization (WHO), the UK's National Health Service (NHS), the US FDA, and Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council have all concluded there is no credible evidence that homeopathy works beyond placebo.

This doesn't mean the people who use it don't feel better — some genuinely do. But the scientific consensus is that this improvement is not caused by the homeopathic remedy itself.
Why It Still Exists and Is Used

Despite scientific rejection, homeopathy remains widely practiced, especially in countries like India, Germany, France, and Brazil. Several reasons explain this:

  • The placebo effect is real and can produce genuine relief.
  • Homeopathic consultations tend to be long, empathetic, and personalised — in itself, this kind of attention can make people feel better.
  • It is perceived as "natural" and safe, so people feel comfortable trying it.
  • It has a long history (it was developed in the late 1700s), giving it cultural weight in many communities.
  • Some people turn to it after conventional medicine fails to relieve their condition.

Homeopathy is not the same as:

  • Herbal medicine — which uses actual plant extracts in meaningful doses, and some of which do have proven pharmacological effects.
  • Naturopathy — a broader alternative health system that may include homeopathy but also covers nutrition, lifestyle, and other approaches.
  • Conventional medicine / allopathy — evidence-based medicine developed through scientific research and clinical trials.

Homeopathy is an alternative medical system that claims diseases can be treated using highly diluted substances that, in their undiluted form, would produce similar symptoms. It operates on principles that contradict established science, and the scientific consensus is that it does not work beyond the placebo effect. However, it has a long history and millions of practitioners and users worldwide, making it culturally and socially significant even if not medically endorsed.
